connection: Production remains synchronous and in-memory through Session 30B. Session 31 deliberately adds SQLite I/O, a separate async repository contract, and EF Core async calls for the first time.
objectives: Add EF Core SQLite to Infrastructure.
Define IAsyncClockEntryRepository with Async suffixes and CancellationToken parameters.
Map ClockEntry to a persistence entity without weakening Domain invariants.
Await FirstOrDefaultAsync and SaveChangesAsync as genuine external I/O.

visuals.title: Domain promise, Infrastructure fulfillment
visuals.explanation: Domain owns a persistence-agnostic async contract. Infrastructure fulfills that promise with EF Core and SQLite.

visuals.title: Options travel into the base context
visuals.explanation: The caller builds options, TimeClockDbContext receives them, and base(options) gives the same configuration to EF Core before the derived constructor body runs.

visuals.title: Tracking precedes database I/O
visuals.explanation: Add marks an entity Added in the context. SaveChangesAsync examines tracked changes and sends the SQL insert.

visuals.title: One real SQLite round trip
visuals.explanation: A Domain ClockEntry becomes an entity row, is inserted and queried through SQLite, then becomes a valid Domain ClockEntry again.

preQuiz.prompt: Who should own a persistence-agnostic repository promise?
preQuiz.explanation: Domain owns the contract; Infrastructure supplies the EF Core implementation.

preQuiz.prompt: Does DbSet.Add immediately execute an SQL insert?
options: No, it marks the entity Added for SaveChanges
preQuiz.explanation: SaveChangesAsync is the genuine database-I/O point.

preQuiz.prompt: Why keep an in-memory SQLite connection open?
options: The database exists for that connection's lifetime
To make Task create a thread
preQuiz.explanation: Closing the connection destroys that in-memory database.

concept.title: Start with one boundary map
paragraphs: Domain owns the promise; Infrastructure fulfills it. The existing synchronous contract remains unchanged while a separate asynchronous contract describes genuine database I/O.
A project reference exposes another project's compiled types. A NuGet package reference supplies external library code and assets.
concept.code: Domain contract → Infrastructure EF repository → SQLite

concept.title: Essential EF vocabulary
paragraphs: An entity represents stored columns. DbContext is one EF Core work session. DbSet<TEntity> is the query-and-save entry point for one entity type, not a List containing every row.
Tracking means the context remembers entity instances and states such as Added, Unchanged, Modified, and Deleted. Materialization is when query results become objects.
concept.code: Add tracks the change. SaveChanges sends the change.

concept.title: Keep Domain rules intact
paragraphs: An invariant is a rule that must remain true for a valid domain object. ClockEntry protects its invariants through its constructor and methods; ClockEntryEntity has settable storage properties so EF can materialize rows.
Mapping back constructs a valid ClockEntry rather than bypassing its rules. Public entity setters do not require Domain to surrender its invariants.

lab.title: Create the First Genuine Asynchronous Persistence Boundary
lab.objective: Persist and retrieve an open ClockEntry through EF Core and SQLite while preserving the Domain boundary.
lab.task: Complete one real round trip: Domain ClockEntry to SQLite row and back to a valid Domain ClockEntry.
lab.startingCondition: Session 30B is complete. Infrastructure still contains only its unused Class1.cs template, and the asynchronous persistence files do not exist yet.

preLabCleanup.text: Verify that src/PinkMachine19.TimeClock.Infrastructure/Class1.cs is still only the unused template placeholder. Delete only that file. This is repository cleanup, not an EF Core learning step.

steps.text: Open a Bash terminal at the learner repository root. Define the descriptive variables shown, then add a project reference from Infrastructure to Domain. These are temporary shell variables, not C# or project-file syntax. The reference lets Infrastructure implement Domain contracts and map to Domain objects.
steps.completeWhen: Infrastructure.csproj contains the Domain ProjectReference and the four Bash variables remain available in that terminal.

steps.text: Add Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore.Sqlite. It supplies DbContext APIs, the SQLite provider, relational behavior, and the async database methods used here.
steps.completeWhen: The package command succeeds and Infrastructure.csproj lists Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore.Sqlite 10.0.10.

steps.text: Add Microsoft.Extensions.DependencyInjection.Abstractions. It supplies DI contracts and registration abstractions without adding the complete container implementation where only abstractions are needed.

Add the selected native SQLite bundle. The repository pins patched SQLitePCLRaw.bundle_e_sqlite3 version 2.1.12 so native SQLite loading is deterministic instead of silently varying with a transitive version.
steps.completeWhen: Infrastructure.csproj lists all three package references at the requested versions.
steps.purposeAfter: Infrastructure can now name Domain contracts and use EF Core's SQLite implementation. The next step defines the persistence promise before any framework-specific class fulfills it.

steps.text: In Domain/Repositories, create IAsyncClockEntryRepository.cs beside IClockEntryRepository. This repository organizes contracts by responsibility; a generic Interfaces folder could work elsewhere but would create a second convention here. Folders organize these global-namespace files but do not automatically create C# namespaces. Declare SaveClockEntryAsync returning Task and GetOpenClockEntryAsync returning Task<ClockEntry?>. Both accept CancellationToken cancellationToken = default.
steps.completeWhen: The interface contains both async signatures at Domain/Repositories/IAsyncClockEntryRepository.cs.

questionsAfter.question: Why does the interface live in Domain?
questionsAfter.answer: Domain owns the persistence-agnostic promise; Infrastructure will fulfill it with EF Core.

questionsAfter.question: Does the Repositories folder create a namespace?
questionsAfter.answer: No. This learner repository uses global namespaces; the folder communicates source responsibility.

steps.purposeAfter: The asynchronous promise now exists, but it has no persistence implementation. Infrastructure will next define the stored shape and EF Core work session.

steps.text: Build the Domain project in Release before adding EF types.
steps.completeWhen: Domain builds with zero errors and the new interface has no missing-return or async warnings.

steps.text: In Infrastructure, create sealed ClockEntryEntity with settable Id, EmployeeId, ClockIn, and nullable Clockout properties. Id is the SQLite-generated row key. Do not add business methods. Remember: an invariant is a rule that must remain true for a valid Domain object; this entity represents columns while Domain ClockEntry continues protecting those rules.
steps.completeWhen: ClockEntryEntity.cs compiles as a storage shape with exactly the four required properties.

questionsAfter.question: Why are the entity setters public when ClockEntry uses private setters?
questionsAfter.answer: EF materializes storage objects through settable properties; Domain still protects business invariants through its own constructor and methods.

questionsAfter.question: Why is Id not a Domain ClockEntry property?
questionsAfter.answer: Id identifies the SQLite row and is generated by persistence; it is not part of this Domain model's business identity.

steps.text: In Infrastructure, create sealed TimeClockDbContext deriving from DbContext. Accept DbContextOptions<TimeClockDbContext> options and forward it with : base(options). The caller created these options; they describe the provider, SQLite connection or connection string, and optional EF behavior—not stored rows. Expose ClockEntries as DbSet<ClockEntryEntity> by returning Set<ClockEntryEntity>().
steps.code:
Caller builds options
→ TimeClockDbContext receives them
→ base(options) forwards them to DbContext
→ EF Core configures the context
→ the derived constructor body runs
steps.completeWhen: TimeClockDbContext has the forwarding constructor and ClockEntries DbSet property.

questionsAfter.question: Who creates the options?
questionsAfter.answer: The composition caller—later, the integration test—builds and passes them.

questionsAfter.question: Has SQL run merely because ClockEntries was accessed?
questionsAfter.answer: No. DbSet begins query/save work; translated queries execute only when materialized.

questionsAfter.question: Is DbSet a List of every row?
questionsAfter.answer: No. It is EF Core's query-and-save entry point for that entity type.

steps.purposeAfter: The storage shape and EF work session now exist, but no repository maps between Domain objects and those persistence objects.

steps.text: Build Infrastructure in Release before writing the repository.
steps.completeWhen: Domain and Infrastructure both build with zero errors.

steps.text: Create sealed EfClockEntryRepository implementing IAsyncClockEntryRepository and inject TimeClockDbContext. Start with warning-free non-async temporary methods: SaveClockEntryAsync returns Task.CompletedTask, and GetOpenClockEntryAsync returns Task.FromResult<ClockEntry?>(null).
steps.completeWhen: The repository shell implements both interface methods and Infrastructure still builds without missing returns or unnecessary async warnings.

steps.text: Implement SaveClockEntryAsync. First add async and remove Task.CompletedTask. Refresh object-initializer grammar with the generic shape shown, then create ClockEntryEntity from EmployeeId, ClockIn, and Clockout. Do not copy Id because SQLite generates it. Call ClockEntries.Add, then await SaveChangesAsync(cancellationToken).
steps.completeWhen: SaveClockEntryAsync maps the Domain entry, marks the entity Added, and awaits SaveChangesAsync with the forwarded token.

questionsAfter.question: Did Add execute an INSERT?
questionsAfter.answer: No. Add changes in-memory tracking state to Added.

questionsAfter.question: Where does genuine database I/O happen?
questionsAfter.answer: SaveChangesAsync examines tracked changes and sends SQL through SQLite.

questionsAfter.question: Does await automatically create another thread?
questionsAfter.answer: No. Await observes asynchronous completion; it does not itself create a thread.

steps.purposeAfter: The repository can now translate and persist a Domain entry. It still needs the reverse path: execute one filtered SQLite query and reconstruct an open Domain entry.

steps.text: Implement GetOpenClockEntryAsync as one complete, compilable step. Add async and remove Task.FromResult. Begin with ClockEntries, add AsNoTracking for read-only intent, filter employeeId and Clockout == null, then await FirstOrDefaultAsync with cancellationToken. EF translates this predicate to SQL; it does not load the whole table first. Return null when no row exists; otherwise construct ClockEntry through its public constructor. Because only open rows are queried, do not call ClockOutEntry.
steps.completeWhen: The method executes the translated query, forwards cancellation, and returns either null or a valid open Domain ClockEntry.

questionsAfter.question: What executes the query?
questionsAfter.answer: FirstOrDefaultAsync materializes the translated SQLite query and returns the first entity or null.

questionsAfter.question: Why AsNoTracking?
questionsAfter.answer: The returned entity is read-only evidence, so the context does not need to remember it for later updates.

questionsAfter.question: Why reconstruct through the Domain constructor?
questionsAfter.answer: The constructor preserves Domain invariants instead of treating the entity's public setters as Domain rules.

steps.purposeAfter: The EF repository now owns persistence mechanics in both directions. The service can stay focused on the business decision: reject a second open entry or save a new one.

steps.text: In Domain/Services, create sealed AsyncClockEntryService and inject IAsyncClockEntryRepository. Add TryClockInAsync returning Task<bool>. Await GetOpenClockEntryAsync with the caller's token; return false when an open entry exists. Otherwise construct ClockEntry, await SaveClockEntryAsync with the same token, and return true.
steps.completeWhen: The service coordinates the acceptance rule and forwards cancellation to both genuine I/O calls without referencing EF Core.

steps.text: Build the full solution in Release before writing the integration test so production errors remain separate from test setup.
steps.completeWhen: The solution builds and the new Domain service has no Infrastructure or EF Core dependency.

steps.text: Modify the test project to reference Infrastructure. Create EfClockEntryRepositoryTests.cs and async Fact SaveAndGetOpenClockEntryAsync_PersistsAndReturnsEntry. Setup code: paste the SQLite connection, open call, options builder with UseSqlite(connection), context construction, EnsureCreatedAsync, and repository construction. Keep the connection open because this in-memory database exists only for that connection's lifetime. UseSqlite selects the provider and connection; EnsureCreatedAsync creates the schema before the first save.
steps.completeWhen: The test reaches a constructed EfClockEntryRepository backed by an open, schema-created in-memory SQLite connection.

questionsAfter.question: Why is this boilerplate pasteable?
questionsAfter.answer: It establishes framework plumbing; the learning evidence is the Domain-to-SQLite round trip.

questionsAfter.question: What happens if the connection closes early?
questionsAfter.answer: The in-memory SQLite database disappears, so later operations cannot observe the saved row.

questionsAfter.question: What does UseSqlite(connection) do?
questionsAfter.answer: It puts the selected SQLite provider and open connection into DbContextOptions.

steps.purposeAfter: The test now owns a real but disposable SQLite boundary. The next step writes the meaningful evidence: save a Domain entry, query it back, and assert the reconstructed Domain state.

steps.text: Learning code: write the test's Arrange, Act, and Assert section. Create a fixed DateTime, employee ID, and open Domain ClockEntry. Await SaveClockEntryAsync, then await GetOpenClockEntryAsync. Assert the result is not null and has the expected EmployeeId, ClockIn, and null Clockout.
steps.code:
Domain ClockEntry
→ mapped entity
→ SQLite insert
→ SQLite query
→ mapped Domain ClockEntry
steps.completeWhen: The test proves one complete SQLite round trip through the repository rather than merely constructing EF objects.

steps.text: Run only EfClockEntryRepositoryTests. If VS Code does not display it, run the list-tests command. Command-line discovery is authoritative for the built assembly; the Testing panel is an editor view. If listed, confirm VS Code is connected to WSL at the repository root, run Test: Refresh Tests, then Developer: Reload Window if needed.
steps.completeWhen: The focused EF repository test passes and command-line discovery lists it.

steps.text: Build PinkMachine19.TimeClock.sln in Release, then run the complete test suite with --no-build. Focused validation proved the SQLite behavior; this final validation checks cumulative solution health. Open Solution Reveal only after both commands pass.
steps.code:
dotnet build PinkMachine19.TimeClock.sln --configuration Release
dotnet test PinkMachine19.TimeClock.sln --configuration Release --no-build
steps.completeWhen: The Release solution builds and the complete test suite passes.
steps.purposeAfter: Session 31 now has focused persistence evidence and cumulative verification. Session 32 may build provider-translated query composition on this established SQLite boundary.

reveals.title: Integration test solution
reveals.text: The framework setup stays visible here only after validation; the learner-authored evidence is the save, query, and assertions.

lab.expectedBehavior: The focused test saves one open Domain ClockEntry through EF Core into SQLite, queries it back without tracking, and reconstructs the expected Domain ClockEntry.
lab.validation: dotnet test tests/PinkMachine19.TimeClock.Domain.Tests/PinkMachine19.TimeClock.Domain.Tests.csproj --configuration Release --filter FullyQualifiedName~EfClockEntryRepositoryTests && dotnet build PinkMachine19.TimeClock.sln --configuration Release && dotnet test PinkMachine19.TimeClock.sln --configuration Release --no-build

expectedFiles.why: Remove only the unused template during pre-lab cleanup.
Reference Domain and add EF Core SQLite dependencies.
Configure the EF Core work session.
Map and persist Domain entries through SQLite.
Reference Infrastructure for the integration test.
Verify the real SQLite round trip.

review: Domain owns the async promise while Infrastructure owns EF mechanics.
Temporary Task implementations keep intermediate builds warning-free.
Add and SaveChangesAsync are described as tracking versus I/O.
The test keeps SQLite setup separate from round-trip learning evidence.
No HTTP, migrations, production DI registration, or Session 32 query API is introduced.

postQuiz.prompt: What does ClockEntries.Add(entity) prove by itself?
options: Only that EF tracks the entity as Added
Executes a translated SQLite query and returns one entity or null
postQuiz.explanation: The provider translates and executes the predicate at materialization.

postQuiz.prompt: Why map an entity back through the ClockEntry constructor?
postQuiz.explanation: Persistence materialization must not bypass Domain validity rules.

reflections: Which project owns the promise and which fulfills it?
At what exact lines does database I/O occur?
Which test lines are framework setup and which prove the round trip?
whatBreaks: Without the Domain contract, Infrastructure leaks into business coordination. Without SaveChangesAsync, Added entities never reach SQLite. Without the open connection, the in-memory database disappears. Without constructor mapping, persistence could bypass Domain validity rules.
summary: Session 31 creates the first genuine asynchronous persistence boundary: Domain defines the promise, Infrastructure maps and performs SQLite I/O, and an integration test proves the complete round trip.
